issues.passage: His decision to challenge the chair’s proposal in open session was an attempt to ingratiate himself with the committee.
issues.why: "Ingratiate himself with the committee" is correct construction and sense (deliberate effort to win favor). Challenging a chair’s proposal can be a calculated way to please a committee that opposes the chair; the sentence is natural, defensible English, not misuse.

fix.correctPassage: Hoping for a promotion, the junior analyst tried to ingratiate herself with the partners by taking on thankless assignments.
wrongPassages: She tried to ingratiate herself with the dean by ignoring every request and missing every meeting.
She managed to ingratiate the rival department by blocking every request for shared resources.
The envoy sought to ingratiate the host government by publicly dismissing its concerns.

issues.passage: The esoteric handbook became required reading in nearly every introductory course.
issues.why: "Esoteric handbook" correctly means specialist-only material. That such a book later became widely assigned does not reverse the adjective; ironic curriculum design still leaves the word used correctly.

fix.correctPassage: The paper’s esoteric methodology limited its readership to specialists in the field.
wrongPassages: The esoteric handbook was assigned because any first-year student could follow it without prior training.
She favored esoteric explanations because they used only everyday vocabulary.
Networks chose esoteric programming precisely for its broad popular appeal.
